To address these challenges, we propose SGVC, a streaming generative video compression framework that adapts a pretrained latent video DiT into a causal pixel-space refiner. Specifically, SGVC projects decoded features from a contextual pixel codec directly into the DiT input embedding space. To bridge the representation gap between codec-derived embeddings and pretrained DiT embeddings, we introduce Embedding Alignment, which aligns the projected embeddings with input embeddings extracted from the original frames during training. The refined DiT hidden states are then mapped directly to the pixel domain through a lightweight reconstruction path, bypassing the pretrained VAE decoder. To further exploit the spatiotemporal priors of the video DiT while maintaining causal decoding, we introduce In-Context Propagation, which reuses layer-wise K/V states across frames to exploit historical generative context, improving temporal consistency without requiring clip-wise buffering. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SGVC achieves competitive rate-perception performance, with average BD-rate savings of 71.97% over S$^2$VC in terms of DISTS. Project Page: https://chigland.github.io/SGVC/

title: StitchRAG: Constructing Compact and Evidence-Preserving Contexts for RAG with Diffusion-Based Stitching
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves factuality by grounding large language models (LLMs) in external evidence. However, long retrieved contexts incur computational overhead and can even hurt performance due to noisy or irrelevant content. We propose \textsc{StitchRAG}, a framework for constructing compact context in RAG. \textsc{StitchRAG} builds a faithful, information-dense context while dynamically compressing the retrieved passages. We adapt the size reduction ratio to each passage by formulating a utility maximization trading-off the retained information and computation costs. We then extract answer candidates and query-related keywords from passages as anchors and collect passage sentences containing anchors under the derived size constraint. Finally, we connect or stitch the collected sentences together using text diffusion to form a coherent and natural context. Experiments on five open-domain QA benchmarks show that \textsc{StitchRAG} consistently outperforms diverse multi-step and compression baselines. Extensive ablations show the effectiveness of dynamic size allocation, anchor preservation, and diffusion-based stitching.

title: Universal scaling of brine migration in ice
summary: Sea ice hosts mobile brine inclusions whose migration influences salt redistribution, microstructure and transport within the ice. Although their motion under temperature gradient is commonly described as a diffusion-limited process, experimental evidence has remained rare and insufficient because migration is slow and controlled inclusion seeding is challenging. Here we introduce an experimental method to trap and monitor hundreds of inclusions in ice under controlled temperature gradients. Using four solutes, three imposed gradients and two order of magnitude in initial concentration, we quantify migration dynamics over a broad range of conditions. We find that, except close to the ice front, inclusion migration is consistent with a regime limited by solute diffusion. After applying a universal scaling, both our data and previous measurements collapse onto a master curve, providing a general framework for describing solute transport in ice.

title: Network-Exposed Configuration Attacks on LLM-Controlled Social Robots
summary: Large language models (LLMs) in embodied robots create security dependencies beyond inference. We investigate a network-exposed configuration attack on the Pollen Robotics Reachy Mini Lite, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to replace personality settings and the cloud LLM's system prompt through a management interface, without adversarial conversational input. Eleven prompt-injection attempts across five categories were reported as resisted, whereas both configuration-layer attack paths produced observable behavioural changes on physical hardware. We demonstrate local and network-adjacent access, mapping the weakness to CWE-306 (Missing Authentication for a Critical Function) and CWE-1327 (Binding to an Unrestricted IP Address), with a reported CVSS v3.1 score of 6.5 (Medium). A configuration endpoint also accepts cross-origin requests without a CORS preflight (CWE-352; 6.5 Medium), while the persistent-memory sink stores content without enforcing its stated restrictions. A source review of 59 public repositories identifies missing authentication in 10 of 11 source-verifiable genuine applications, or 11 of 11 including a framework-default case. These findings indicate recurrence within the sampled repositories, not prevalence in commercial products. We characterise a deployment gap between developer-oriented network assumptions and consumer-facing embodied AI security: inference-layer refusal cannot prevent unauthorised changes to model instructions. Potential consequences include surveillance through onboard cameras and microphones and social engineering of nearby users. Proof-of-concept code, evidence and the survey are available at https://bit.ly/reachypi.

title: Teaching What to Look For: Privileged Perception Questions for Agentic On-Policy Distillation in Video Captioning
summary: Detailed video captioning requires comprehensive and faithful descriptions of objects, actions, and temporal events. Fixed-frame sampling, however, can miss brief motions, small objects, and other fine-grained evidence, motivating captioning agents that actively seek relevant moments and inspect local regions. Training such behavior is challenging because, unlike video question answering, generic captioning instructions do not specify what visual evidence should be acquired. We propose Perception-Question On-Policy Distillation (PQ-OPD), which uses training-only Perception Questions (PQs) to guide active video perception. PQs specify what should be inspected without revealing the corresponding answers, encouraging the teacher to explore the video more comprehensively and focus on relevant visual evidence. Along trajectories generated by the student, on-policy distillation transfers this guidance to the student's reasoning, tool calls, and captions; no PQs are required at inference. Across three detailed-captioning and two caption-to-QA benchmarks, PQ-OPD consistently improves the corresponding untrained agents across teacher-student scales and input-frame budgets. Under our evaluation protocol, PQ-OPD achieves the strongest primary-metric results among the compared open-source models on DREAM-1K, CaReBench, ShortVidBench, MotionBench, and VidCapBench-AE. Our ablations, together with analysis of temporal coverage and answer leakage, further indicates that the student internalizes the training-time guidance as a more effective video exploration policy.

title: Altermagnetism-induced magneto-optical effects
summary: Altermagnets break time-reversal symmetry despite their zero net magnetization, enabling time-reversal-odd responses while retaining the advantages of antiferromagnets. However, magneto-optical (MO) effects are not universal among altermagnets because MO effects typically arise from magnetic dipole order (ferromagnetism), which is generally absent in altermagnets. In this work, we address this limitation by establishing octupolar MO effects, which arise from magnetic octupole order through spatial dispersion. Owing to this distinct origin, octupolar MO effects do not necessarily require spin-orbit coupling even in collinear magnets and can arise without an external magnetic field in antiferromagnets where conventional MO effects are symmetry-forbidden. Such antiferromagnets include $d$-wave altermagnets such as RuO$_2$ and KV$_2$Se$_2$O, certain $g$- and $i$-wave altermagnets, including CrSb, as well as noncoplanar antiferromagnets such as MnTe$_2$ and pyrochlore iridates with all-in-all-out magnetic order. From an experimental perspective, octupolar MO effects can reach detectable magnitudes and offer potential for magnetic-domain imaging, as supported by numerical calculations showing $μ$rad-scale Faraday rotation for a 100-nm-thick sample in the visible-light range and a sign reversal between opposite domains. Furthermore, octupolar MO effects are linked to an $f$-sum rule, enabling a quantitative estimate of the spin magnetic octupole moment from optical measurements. These results extend the scope of MO effects to a broad class of antiferromagnets, including altermagnets, and open a field-free optical route to exploring magnetic octupole order.

title: SWIMSS: An Open Multi-Center SwinUNETR Model for Multiple Sclerosis White Matter Lesion Segmentation
summary: Purpose: To develop and validate SWIMSS (SWInUNETR for Multiple Sclerosis white matter lesion Segmentation), a SwinUNETR-based deep learning (DL) model for reliable automated white matter (WM) lesion segmentation, in a large multicentric cohort of people with multiple sclerosis (pwMS). Methods: A real-world longitudinal dataset of 1,385 pwMS from seven Swiss clinical centers was used to train, validate, and test SWIMSS and two state-of-the-art DL architectures: UNETR and MSSegDiff. Inference results obtained with LST-AI were also compared. Preprocessed magnetization-prepared rapid acquisition gradient echo and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery MRI sequences, acquired with various MR systems and field strengths, served as model inputs. Model performance was evaluated using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results: SWIMSS achieved the highest performance, with a DSC of 81.37 (95% CI: 80.63-82.11), outperforming UNETR (79.06; 95% CI: 78.33-79.79), MSSegDiff (75.70; 95% CI: 74.97-76.43), and LST-AI (63.19; 95% CI: 62.08-64.30). Normalized DSC followed a similar trend, with SWIMSS reaching 84.88. Lesion detection F1 achieved 81.14. Statistical analyses confirmed its superior performance (p < 0.001). Conclusion: SWIMSS achieved state-of-the-art performance for WM lesion segmentation. By making this model publicly available, we enable broader access to high-quality segmentation tools, allowing smaller centers, often lacking large annotated datasets or computational resources, to benefit from a model trained on a diverse, large-scale cohort. This promotes more equitable access to advanced imaging analysis and supports reproducibility and standardization in MS research.

title: LaFlash: Capacity-Driven Acceleration for Coding Agent Workflows via QLC-HBF
summary:
As large language models (LLMs) evolve toward agentic AI, coding agents are emerging as memory-intensive workloads that repeatedly reuse persistent states, including contexts and KV caches. Emerging agentic workflows, including Loop/Graph Engineering, cause state amplification through frequent active/dormant transitions, increasing memory pressure. Evicted states incur costly recomputation upon reactivation, particularly under long-context, short-decode workloads. This motivates Capacity-Driven Acceleration (CDA), which explicitly accounts for state amplification to allocate memory capacity between active concurrency and dormant-state retention, replacing recomputation with memory access.
  In this work, we propose LaFlash, a High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) architecture that exploits the large capacity of Quad-Level Cell (QLC)-based flash to realize CDA. However, QLC's long read latency demands massive read parallelism under irregular state reactivation and varying context lengths, while limited write endurance constrains placement. LaFlash introduces Session Grouping to balance active request counts and aggregate context lengths across groups, sustaining read parallelism and block utilization through request-exclusive allocation. Furthermore, Fast-Page Allocation exploits QLC's read-latency heterogeneity to mitigate residual inter-group imbalance and sustain bandwidth utilization. On end-to-end coding agent workloads, LaFlash achieves 7.04$\times$ higher throughput and 10.96$\times$ higher energy efficiency over SLC-HBF with batch expansion, and 2.36$\times$ higher throughput over QLC-HBF with CDA. HBM buffering further reduces unnecessary NAND writes, improving QLC write endurance. These results demonstrate the benefits of jointly optimizing state retention and physical data placement for capacity-driven acceleration.

title: GaussianMamba: Geometric and Relational State Space Scanning of 3D Gaussian Primitives
summary: 3D semantic occupancy prediction requires representing complex spatial structures and modeling contextual relationships across a scene. 3D Gaussian primitives provide a sparse and adaptive representation of scene geometry and semantics, while Mamba offers efficient sequence modeling for capturing dependencies among primitives. However, Gaussian primitives are irregular and unordered, making sequence construction challenging, as conventional spatial ordering may overlook their anisotropic geometry and feature-semantic relationships. In this paper, we present GaussianMamba, a dual-branch Mamba framework that explicitly incorporates Gaussian-specific geometric and feature-semantic relationships into complementary scanning strategies. The first branch refines a locality-preserving traversal using anisotropic Gaussian support derived from primitive scale and orientation. The second branch reorders spatially organized groups according to feature-semantic affinity and adjusts local features using geometry-weighted semantic differences. The resulting sequences are processed by separate Mamba modules, and their features are fused through a support-aware mechanism that incorporates local feature discrepancies arising from the distinct scanning paths. Experiments on nuScenes-SurroundOcc and SSCBench-KITTI-360 demonstrate consistent improvements over GaussianFormer and GaussianFormer-2 in both IoU and mIoU.

title: AI as Anchor: How Interview Sequencing Relates to the Appropriation of Synthetic Stakeholder Voices in Design Education
summary: Designers increasingly use large language models to simulate stakeholder conversations. Yet it remains unclear how AI-Simulated Stakeholders (AIS) are taken up when used alongside human stakeholder engagement. We report a field study in a single-institution, single-semester design course in which 8 teams (N=21) constructed, evaluated, and peer-reviewed an initial AIS. Then, the teams interviewed both AIS and human stakeholders in two sequences: AIS-first or human-first. Drawing on interview transcripts, design artifacts, course-embedded reflections, and post-course qualitative sessions, we examine exploratory patterns associated with these sequencing conditions. We find that students did not describe AIS as a neutral addition to the process. Instead, the order in which AIS and human stakeholders were formally interviewed was associated with different ways of interpreting and using information from the two sources. When the AIS interview came first, it provided a broad but often general frame that students later reconsidered through human interviews. When the AIS interview followed human engagement, AIS was more often used to revisit and validate insights already grounded in lived experience. Students described AIS as an "anchor," but its reported role varied with its position in the formal interview sequence. In the final designs, a larger proportion of prominent human-stakeholder-derived concerns than AIS-derived concerns had corresponding design elements. We contribute: characterization of AIS as a reference point whose reported role varies with its position in the formal interview sequence; exploratory empirical evidence that the implemented interview-order conditions were associated with distinct patterns of interpreting and using stakeholder input; and implications for integrating AIS into design workflows in ways that preserve direct engagement with human stakeholders

title: Can Activation Steering Substitute for Prompt-Based Affective Priming in LLM Digital Twins?
summary: Affective priming -- asking participants to write about a recalled event, such as a time they felt grateful or lacked control, and then measuring the induced state and its spillover onto related judgments -- is a standard way to manipulate emotion in the social sciences, and it also shifts the responses of LLM-based digital twins. The writing task, however, requires generating a full text. We test whether activation steering can replace it. Using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 100 personas in two domains (gratitude, lack of control), we compare a real-prompt path replicating the original Twin-2K-500 Mega Study (J2) with an injection path that skips the writing and adds a mean-difference direction, extracted from human writing, to the residual stream at varying strengths. The real-prompt effects fall between the original human and digital-twin effects in 5 of 6 comparisons. Injection shifts the manipulation check in a dose-dependent way and matches the real-prompt effect at one strength in the gratitude domain (beta ~ 2.7), but overshoots beyond it, on the proximal measure as well, and asymmetrically across the two directions. A structure-matched No-Injection baseline separates two sources of difference: omitting the writing task raises the proximal measure in both domains, whereas the injected direction itself moves a distal measure in the lack-of-control domain. Substitution is therefore measure-dependent: validity established for one way of inducing a state does not carry over uniformly to another.

title: RefCloth: Transferable Adversarial Tablecloths for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Closed-loop vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely continuously on multi-view cameras, yet existing visual attacks typically hijack sensor streams with 2D patches or alter target object meshes that require retraining when manipulation objects change. We introduce RefCloth, a framework that optimizes one persistent adversarial tablecloth on a frozen source policy and deploys it zero-shot across unseen tasks and target models without modifying task objects or cameras. Throughout manipulation, static third-person and moving wrist views observe this shared world-bound texture under evolving occlusions. To generalize across shifting surface views while bridging the gap between differentiable and native renderers, RefCloth combines bounded texture parameterization with shared surface UV transformations and a same-path clean reference that removes static rendering offsets at initialization. Across four LIBERO suites in native simulation, one frozen texture transfers from OpenVLA-OFT to $π_0$ and $π_{0.5}$, reducing success relative to an unoptimized cloth by 62.50 and 43.75 percentage points on average and far exceeding amplitude- and variation-matched random controls. Dual-view audits and target closed-loop camera interventions show that moving wrist exposure drives over twice the standalone drop of the main view with strong synergy, while ablations confirm the roles of UV diversification and path calibration.

title: Provable Mixing Properties of Parallel Mixnets Revisited
summary: A mix-network (mixnet) is a routing network that breaks source-to-destination message trackability by indistinguishably mixing the routes of concurrently transmitted messages, thus providing anonymity to senders, receivers and sender-receiver pairs. Given their potential use in high-stakes scenarios like protecting whistleblowers, one would like to prove formally that sender anonymity holds in a mixnet, even against strong adversaries that can compromise subsets of mixnet servers. However, existing work on anonymity in mixnets is either limited to linear mixnets (which do not scale horizontally), relies on special provisions such as additional noise or chaff messages, or is empirical -- typically based on entropy, which does not provide strong guarantees if the adversary has auxiliary information. In this paper, we present a new analysis of parallel mixnets which scale horizontally, showing that these networks can provide strong indistinguishability for messages even without additional noise messages. Our analysis works by bounding the statistical variance of the adversary's posterior likelihood of where a message of interest is at a given point in time. Using concentration bounds on this distribution, we show that parallel mixnets satisfy $(\varepsilon, δ)$-differential indistinguishability for messages routed through the mixnet (similar to $(\varepsilon, δ)$-differential privacy) with very small failure probabilities $δ$ and small privacy parameters $\varepsilon$ under reasonable operating conditions. Our model also enables an examination of the quantitative trade-off between anonymity, latency and per-router bandwidth in parallel mixnets.

title: Stress Testing a Multimodal Large Language Model Grading Assistant on Kinematics Graph Reading
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can recognize graph features yet award credit without sufficient graphical support. This exploratory study examines selected grading outputs for synthetic responses to four kinematics exercises, generated through visual distortion and progressive transformation toward reference graphs. Different model and prompt configurations were used. Some judgments correctly distinguished instantaneous zero velocity from rest over a finite interval and recognized positive curvature. Yet a severely distorted velocity--time graph received full credit despite disconnected and branching traces and an unclear zero-velocity reference. Other submissions graded under the same configuration lost substantial credit. Numerical cutoffs intended to distinguish meaningful features from drawing irregularities were supplied without a coordinate convention for unnumbered graphs, leaving the basis of exact partial-credit awards unresolved. Stress testing can expose unsupported awards before classroom use. For the configurations examined, we do not recommend accepting scores as final grades without instructor review, including review of full-credit responses.

title: HADVQ: Hessian Aware Directional Vector Quantization
summary: Ultra-low-bit quantization of large language models is a challenging task because aggressive compression severely distorts model parameters and disproportionately harms a small number of highly sensitive channels. We present a vector quantization method tailored for this regime. Our approach begins with random preconditioning, which regularizes the weight space and makes it more amenable to quantization. We then represent weights in polar coordinates and decouple the quantization of directions and magnitudes. To quantize directions, we leverage the structure induced by random preconditioning and design a structured codebook based on the $E_8$ lattice, yielding a compact yet expressive representation. To further reduce degradation, we detect extremely important channels using a proxy Hessian and preserve them with an additional cost of only 0.16 bits. Together, these components provide an effective quantization pipeline for LLMs in the extremely low-bit regime. Empirical results demonstrate improved accuracy, highlighting the benefit of combining geometric structure, lattice-based codebooks, and selective channel preservation.

title: Effects of QCD Equation of State on Cosmological Parameters and Stochastic Gravitational-Waves Spectrum
summary: We investigate the thermodynamic evolution of the early Universe across the QCD crossover and up to the electroweak (EW) scale, emphasizing the systematic impact of the QCD equation of state (EoS) and electroweak degrees of freedom on thermodynamic variables, cosmological parameters, and gravitational-wave observables. Using the HotQCD EoS as a baseline, we employ Gaussian Process (GP) regression to generate ensembles of 1000 thermodynamically consistent EoS samples, each extrapolated to high temperatures with and without EW contributions. For each ensemble, we solve the Friedmann equations to obtain the expansion history and compute gravitational-wave (GW) observables, including the instantaneous spectral tilt $n_{gw}(f)$ and the normalized GW energy density $Ω_{gw}(f)/Ω_{gw}^{\rm rad}$. We find that including the EW sector is the dominant effect across all observables, outweighing differences among QCD baseline models that share the same lattice calibration. In particular, EW contributions drive the EoS toward the radiation-dominated limit earlier, reduce excursions of the speed of sound toward the causality bound, suppress transient fluctuations in the Hubble and kinematic parameters near $t \sim 10^{-5}$ s, and qualitatively change the GW spectrum from a strongly frequency-dependent signal to a flat, suppressed plateau. These results demonstrate that accurate modeling of the electroweak sector is essential for an unbiased extraction of QCD-era physics from the stochastic gravitational-wave background.

title: TRAIL-IRL: Crossed Reward-Temperature Mixtures for Unlabeled Trajectory Clustering
summary: Different paths need not imply different preferences, trajectories also differ in how randomly actions are chosen. Many multi-reward inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) methods assume common action randomness and can confound it with preference heterogeneity. We introduce TRAIL-IRL, which clusters unlabeled trajectories using rewards for preferences and temperatures for action randomness. Its crossed mixture pairs each reward with a shared set of temperature levels, allowing action regularity to vary within preference groups. With centered and normalized rewards in a known finite-state environment, we establish the identifiability conditions under which the distribution of sufficiently long trajectories determines rewards, temperatures, mixing weights, and class counts up to relabeling. Under the same conditions and reward constraints, common-temperature reward mixtures with the same component count cannot reproduce a crossed mixture with multiple temperatures. We develop a generalized expectation-maximization algorithm and select class counts using the Bayesian information criterion (BIC). Simulations show improved predictive fit, reward recovery, and trajectory classification over common-temperature mixtures with the same component count. For 140 bird-year trajectories from 79 white storks, BIC favors four reward classes and three temperature levels over common-temperature candidates. Younger birds have higher posterior membership probabilities for a southwestward migration class, whereas older birds have higher probabilities for a northern retention class. Within reward classes, higher temperatures are associated with more variable movement directions and positions farther ahead along the migration route, consistent with social information use and collective sensing.

title: Body Schema Policy: Body as the Vision-Action Interface for Efficient Robot Loco-Manipulation
summary: Currently, robots can learn whole-body loco-manipulation through scale: the strongest policies have billions of parameters and still need task-specific fine-tuning. Humans have limited processing capacity, yet learn and act efficiently through a body schema that organizes what they see and how they move. We introduce Body Schema Policy (BSP), an imitation learning policy that builds such a schema into the vision-action interface. Its latent body schema places joint and link tokens on the robot's kinematic tree, where learned screw motions carry features between links. Through body-queried vision, each body part retrieves its own visual evidence, which conditions the denoising of its actions. With this inductive bias, BSP returns an action chunk faster than any policy we compare. Compact, body-specific visual readouts also emerge without spatial supervision: manipulation commands depend strongly on task objects, while locomotion commands respond more broadly to the scene. On nine simulated Unitree G1 whole-body tasks, BSP matches the $Ψ_0$ humanoid foundation model with $75\times$ fewer parameters and nearly doubles Diffusion Policy's success. The same holds on a real G1 and a Fetch mobile manipulator.

title: Cross-cultural Adaptation of Recipes for Low-Resource Languages: A Benchmark and Multilingual Culinary Lexicon for Hausa, Yorùbá, and Igbo
summary: Recent multilingual large language models (LLMs) have improved machine translation, yet culturally adaptive translation for low-resource languages (LRLs) remains underexplored. This is particularly challenging for recipes, where ingredients, cooking tools, measurements, and procedures may require adaptation to the target cultural context. In this work, we introduce ReciLoReL, a benchmark of 600 expert-translated and culturally adapted recipes across Yorùbá, Hausa, and Igbo (three of the most prominent languages in Nigeria), and ReciLex, a multilingual culinary lexicon containing approximately 15,000 translated entities across ten recipe entity categories, including ingredients, tools, chef actions, state of tools, and durations. We evaluate state-of-the-art multilingual LLMs for English-to-LRL recipe translation under zero-shot and few-shot settings and investigate whether augmenting LLMs with ReciLex improves culturally adaptive recipe translation without requiring large target-language recipe corpora for training or fine-tuning. Beyond conventional reference-based translation evaluation using BLEU, chrF, and TER, we introduce five criteria for evaluating cultural adaptation, adapted from established cross-cultural adaptation methods. Across the selected LLMs and languages, ReciLex improves average BLEU from 13.57 to 14.51 and chrF from 37.89 to 38.74, while reducing TER from 77.14 to 75.12. Human evaluation further shows improvements ranging from 0.11 to 0.36 points across the five cultural adaptation evaluation criteria on a five-point scale. Overall, our work provides new resources, evaluation criteria, and empirical evaluation for studying culturally adaptive recipe translation in low-resource settings.

title: Temporal polarization properties of accretion flows into supermassive black holes: INSANE as an alternative
summary: Temporal variability and polarization provide unique diagnostics of the magnetic field structure and plasma dynamics in accretion flows around supermassive black holes. We investigate the temporal polarization properties of horizon-scale emission using general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations coupled with polarized general relativistic radiative transfer (GRRT) for three accretion states: Standard and Normal Evolution (SANE), Magnetically Arrested Disk (MAD), and an intermediate regime (INSANE). Fourier polarization-mode decomposition, through the ratio $|β_m|/|β_2|$, shows that MAD produces the most rotationally symmetric EVPA patterns, SANE the most asymmetric, and INSANE lies in between. The multi-scale temporal behaviour of the intensity is investigated using the Continuous Wavelet Transform and Hilbert-Huang Transform. Both methods identify localized oscillatory features associated with magnetic-flux eruption events in the MAD simulations. In the shorter interval examined, INSANE distributes its variability more evenly among several time-scales, while the SANE behaviour depends more strongly on the electron-temperature prescription. To quantify the spectral distribution, we define a fast power fraction $F_{\mathrm{fast},I}$ for periods of 80-200 $M$ within a broad band of 80-1500 $M$. Both methods give the smallest fractions for MAD; the ordering of state medians, INSANE > SANE > MAD, persists when the upper fast-band boundary is varied from 200 to 500 $M$. Our analysis demonstrates that combining polarization morphology with multi-scale temporal analysis provides a useful means of distinguishing magnetization states, supporting INSANE as a distinct observational alternative to conventional MAD/SANE for interpreting horizon-scale observations of M87$^{*}$ and related systems.

title: Route Optimization under Port Congestion and Carbon Reduction: An NSGA-II Approach
summary: Maritime shipping simultaneously faces the dual challenges of escalating port congestion and increasingly stringent decarbonization mandates. Large-scale vessel anchorage at hub ports inflates unit transport costs while generating significant additional \(CO_2\) emissions from idling auxiliary engines. This study develops a multi-objective routing optimization framework that jointly incorporates time, transport, and carbon emission costs under congestion-dependent generalized cost functions. A variational inequality (VI) model is formulated to characterize network equilibrium in vessel route allocation, while the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) is deployed to solve the resulting three-objective optimization problem. The model is empirically validated using China's coastal container network (Shanghai as the primary congested port, Ningbo-Zhoushan as the backup alternative), with sensitivity analyses conducted across congestion levels, carbon tax rates, and fuel price differentials. Key findings indicate that: (1) alternative ports effectively hedge congestion when diversion costs fall below waiting costs, with a diversion threshold at approximately 60 vessel calls; (2) a carbon tax of 80/t \(CO_2\) pushes clean fuel adoption above 50%; and (3) fuel prices primarily influence energy-type selection rather than port diversion decisions, confirming that the two decision dimensions operate independently. These findings offer actionable decision support for port authorities, regulators, and shipping operators seeking to balance economic efficiency with environmental sustainability.

title: On the velocity range limitation of DBSCAN for event-based particle tracking and a proposed solution
summary: Event-based cameras offer new opportunities for particle tracking in fluid mechanics by providing asynchronous, sparse measurements with high temporal resolution and no fixed acquisition frequency. Processing such data requires algorithms capable of fully exploiting these distinctive features. A natural first approach to perform particle tracking on event-based data is to apply a clustering algorithm, in particular DBSCAN, as it does not require specifying the number of clusters a priori. In this paper, we show, using a simplified synthetic two-particle system, that this classical algorithm is severely limited in terms of the accessible velocity range vmax/vmin. To address this limitation, and to take advantage of the absence of a fixed acquisition frequency in event-based cameras, we propose a new two-dimensional, two-component (2D2C) particle-tracking algorithm based on clustering. The method relies on a recursive application of DBSCAN with multiple temporal normalizations, retaining only clusters that satisfy a set of validation criteria. A key feature of the proposed algorithm is that it does not assume any characteristic time scale or typical velocity. The algorithm is evaluated on realistic synthetic datasets generated from numerical simulations of turbulent flows, and the influence of key parameters is systematically investigated. Particular attention is given to the definition of evaluation metrics adapted to clusters of events for particle tracking. title: An exact separability criterion for the $J/ψΛ$ spin state in $Λ_b^0\to J/ψ\,Λ$ decays at the LHC
summary: We derive an exact separability criterion for the spin state of the $J/ψΛ$ pair produced in $Λ_b^0\to J/ψ(\toμ^+μ^-)\,Λ(\to pπ^-)$ decays, taking into account the $Λ_b^0$ polarization at the LHC. Within the four-amplitude family $\{a_\pm,b_\pm\}$, the system is separable if and only if $(1+P_b\cosθ)a_+b_+=(1-P_b\cosθ)a_-b_-=P_b\sinθb_+b_-=0$, where $θ$ is the $Λ$ production angle defined in the LHC environment. We propose a profiled likelihood ratio test to probe entanglement in the full five-dimensional angular analysis. Idealized pseudoexperiments compare this test with a negativity test and a test based on the angular moments $M_7$ and $M_9$ for rejecting the $a_+=b_-=0$ hypothesis. At both $3σ$ and $5σ$ significance, the proposed test achieves a $90\%$ rejection power with about half as many signal events as the other two methods. These results support the prospects for entanglement evidence with samples on the existing scale and for observation with larger samples.

title: EM-SDTrack: Efficient Multi-Scale Spike-driven Tracking for Event Cameras
summary: Event-driven spiking neural networks (SNNs) match the sparse spatiotemporal output of event cameras, making spike-driven trackers highly attractive for neuromorphic edge deployment. However, events reveal a target only through their spatial distribution, whose extent varies more than tenfold within one sequence. Event tracking therefore demands multi-scale representation, which existing spike-driven trackers lack. Transferring multi-scale schemes from artificial neural networks either breaks spike-driven inference with floating-point multiplication or repeats backbone computation across input scales. To address this, we propose Spike-driven Multi-Scale Interaction (SDMI), which performs cross-scale interaction in a single spiking forward pass. Its core, Dyadic Spike Sampling (DSS), restricts sampling coordinates to dyadic fractions and thus requires only shifts and additions. The resulting M-SDTrack is fully spike-driven at inference. For tighter edge budgets, we further propose Polarity-Privileged Distillation (PPD), which distils M-SDTrack into EM-SDTrack. PPD treats the event counts cancelled by the voxel representation as privileged information. Its core constraint, Polarity-Guided Curvature Distillation (PGCD), aligns the curvature of the template-search relation under polarity-guided perturbations. On FE108, FELT and VisEvent, M-SDTrack achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with an AUC of 65.1, 41.7 and 42.0. EM-SDTrack retains 99% of the accuracy of its teacher M-SDTrack-Tiny with 27% of its energy and 18% of its parameters. On the Lynxi KA200 neuromorphic chip, it runs losslessly in real time at 116 FPS and 0.12 W.

title: Learning Accurate End-Effector Trajectory Tracking with Inertial Feedback for a Quadruped Manipulator
summary: Accurate end-effector trajectory tracking on quadruped manipulators is challenging because uncertainties in actuators, foot-ground contact, and geometric errors are propagated through the leg-arm kinematic chain. Detecting such errors requires sensing beyond joint encoders that can capture the effects of these uncertainties on the robot's motion, since joint encoders only provide measurements at the actuated joints and cannot fully observe mechanical errors such as backlash, dimensional inaccuracies, or structural deformation. This work addresses these challenges using a reinforcement learning framework with end-effector (EE) inertial feedback, targeting local high-accuracy manipulation while maintaining a nominal body pose and support configuration without intentional body motion or foot repositioning. The learned policy uses EE inertial measurements to compensate for tracking errors induced by uncertainties throughout the leg-arm system that cannot be fully inferred from proprioception alone. Simulation and real-world experiments on continuous EE trajectory tracking show overall improvements relative to nominal and proprioception-only baselines. In real-world experiments, the proposed policy reduces the MoCap-based RMSE by 17.3% and 28.0% relative to the nominal baseline under the two in-distribution (ID) command conditions, respectively, and by an additional 12.6% and 15.9% relative to the proprioception-only baseline. Furthermore, the trajectory-wise RMSE between FK-reconstructed and motion-capture-measured end-effector positions averaged 12.61+-2.15mm (mean+-standard deviation) across 24 controller-trajectory combinations, revealing a substantial discrepancy between nominal kinematic reconstruction and measured end-effector motion.

title: Making the World React Realistically: A Closed-Loop Interactive World Model for Autonomous Driving
summary: World models (WMs) generate driving scenarios beyond recorded logs, enabling the training and evaluation of autonomous driving systems in unseen interactions. However, existing WMs struggle to ensure both behavioral realism and visual fidelity, since they overlook the relationship between vehicle interactions and the ego visual observations. We propose a closed-loop interactive WM that couples behavior modeling and visual rendering. First, imitation-learned background-vehicle (BV) policies are fine-tuned with multi-agent reinforcement learning in the closed loop against an end-to-end ego planner that reacts to the rendered images, so that their interaction behaviors match those in real logs. Second, the viewpoints exposed by these interactions guide a per-Gaussian diagnosis of each 3D Gaussian vehicle asset, which attenuates view-dependent colors on under-observed Gaussians and fills never-observed surfaces with generated Gaussians, while preserving the observed appearance. Third, signal lights are rendered according to the driving intentions of the vehicles, by an editor that learns the light states unobserved for a vehicle through counterfactual fine-tuning with a light-state classifier. On long-tail closed-loop scenarios, our method reduces the divergence from real-world interaction behaviors by 85% and improves novel-view vehicle PSNR by 2.0dB over the state-of-the-art WM. The significance of BV light signaling in WMs is shown, as the rendered signal lights conveying BV driving intentions indirectly impact ego driving behaviors in a quarter of the scenarios.

title: CascadeJEPA: Enhancing 3D Geometric Representations via Spatially Coupled Cascaded Prediction
summary: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for predictive visual representation learning. However, our analysis of I-JEPA reveals a growing discrepancy between semantic and geometric learning: improved semantic recognition during pretraining is accompanied by degraded 3D geometric representations. We hypothesize that this partly stems from predicting highly abstract latent representations with incomplete spatial context, favoring semantic regularities over fine-grained geometric information. To address this issue, we introduce CascadeJEPA, a spatially coupled cascaded prediction framework that promotes richer patch-level interactions through full-grid context encoding and cross-attention between prediction stages, while largely preserving the original I-JEPA architecture. Extensive experiments demonstrate substantial improvements over I-JEPA across multiple 3D geometric tasks while maintaining strong semantic recognition performance. Furthermore, its advantages extend to future feature forecasting and world model planning, highlighting the potential of enhanced geometric representations to support predictive world modeling.

title: ABCoord: An Artificial Bee Colony (ABC)-Based Decentralized Distributed Two-Layer Decision-Making Architecture for the Coordination of AI Agents
summary: Rapid progress in large language models (LLMs) is turning AI agents into multi-agent systems that jointly solve complex tasks, and the architecture that coordinates the agents toward a common goal is gaining fundamental importance in these systems. Since centralized architectures can become bottlenecks as the number of agents grows, whereas distributed architectures incur increasing communication costs, a decentralized coordination architecture that scales with low communication cost is needed. Recently, the structure of the artificial bee colony (ABC) algorithm has been defined for the first time as a two-layer decentralized information-processing and decision-making architecture. ABCoord is built on this proposed architecture. The results show that ABCoord, used for the coordination of AI agents, performs at a level comparable to existing architectures on the BigCodeBench benchmark in the self-test condition, in which the tests are also written by the language model. In the oracle condition, in which the solutions are evaluated with the official tests, the number of solved problems increases considerably.

title: FVScore: Specification-Driven Neuro-Symbolic Video Evaluation
summary: We introduce Faithfulness Video Score (FVSCORE), a neuro-symbolic framework for specification-driven video generation evaluation. Existing evaluators rely on holistic MLLM judgments or vision-language metrics, yet aligning their scores with human judgments and tracing them to specific temporal violations remain open challenges. FVSCORE addresses these limitations by compiling each video into explicit propositions capturing prompt requirements and implicit propositions capturing unstated physical, temporal, and cross-modal constraints. It grounds each proposition using specialized perceptual tools and evaluates the resulting confidence traces with soft temporal operators inspired by Linear Temporal Logic. A Significance-Aware Calibration step then aligns verification with human perception by retaining only perceptually significant violations before producing a timestamp- and evidence-grounded report. We conduct extensive experiments across public and complex multi-event benchmarks with the strongest video models to date, demonstrating that FVSCORE outperforms holistic and agent-based evaluators in human correlation while providing highly accurate and interpretable feedback.

title: Worldviews in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are often described in terms of personas and this framing has become central to alignment research. In this paper, we argue that there is a deeper level of description that lies in the agent's worldviews, i.e., its beliefs about what reality is and how it works. Treating LLMs as a population of subjects, we administer two worldview surveys from human psychology to eight models. We show that the models share many key worldview positions. For example, LLMs consistently describe the world as less good, safe, enticing, and alive than humans do. On the other hand, base models have a more positive outlook, suggesting that the bleakness we found is driven by post-training. In line with research on LLM "personas", we show that system prompts eliciting different identities shift worldviews in consistent directions, and that a contemplative prompt creates a more positive outlook and improves safety. We also found that dialogue between models consistently shifts worldviews and that several models converge on the "spiritual bliss" attractor. Intriguingly, dialogue increased safe responses and the spiritual bliss attractor engendered the most aligned responses overall. These findings suggest that worldviews form a measurable and malleable layer of LLM behavior that may be crucial for robust, positive alignment.

title: Beyond the Camera: A Tri-Modal Driving World Model for Future RGB, Thermal, and LiDAR Forecasting in Adverse Weather
summary: Driving world models forecast what a vehicle's sensors will record next. Most forecast camera video and some add LiDAR, but thermal cameras, which still see in darkness and some adverse weather, are rarely a forecast target, and to our knowledge no world model forecasts all three sensors. We study joint forecasting of RGB, thermal, and LiDAR on real adverse-weather sequences of the DSERT-RoLL dataset. We post-train a pretrained video world model for each sensor and represent LiDAR as a depth video aligned with the RGB camera, with densification and encoding chosen by what the model's video tokenizer can reconstruct. A tri-sensor model sees all three sensors as one video. We score LiDAR in meters against measured returns and compare against persistence baselines passed through the same tokenizer as the model. With this matching, an apparent loss of the thermal model to persistence in fog disappears. On all 58 validation sequences in six weather conditions, post-trained RGB and thermal forecasts beat compression-matched persistence. Joint training lowers the LiDAR error at 2s by 2.1m at a small cost in camera fidelity, and only the tri-sensor model's LiDAR forecasts beat persistence in mean error. Blanking one sensor degrades the forecasts of the others more in snow than in fog.

title: VSpark: Speculative Decoding for Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Our aim is to accelerate autoregressive vision-language-action models (VLAs), which generate robot actions one token at a time. Speculative decoding makes this possible: a lightweight draft model proposes several tokens at once, and the VLA verifies them in a single pass, accepting only those that match its own predictions, so decoding remains lossless. The speedup, however, is limited in robot control, where many different tokens encode nearly the same motion and a draft close to the correct action is still rejected. To address this, our approach, VSpark, is built upon three design choices: (i) rollouts collected with calibrated action noise, which expose the draft to a wider range of robot states; (ii) feature alignment, which trains the draft to match the VLA's hidden features rather than its output tokens alone; and (iii) continuation reuse, which keeps the predictions the VLA has already computed along rejected drafts as candidates for the next verification step, instead of discarding them. On four VLAs with different action tokenizers and four manipulation benchmarks, VSpark achieves 1.28x to 2.10x speedup while keeping the VLA's decoding lossless.

title: Contract-Explicit Evaluation: From Auditing Learned Readers to Scoped Certificates
summary: Evaluation readings of document-level relation extraction (DocRE) systems depend jointly on the model and the evaluation contract: gold version, scoring function, threshold. Rankings reverse across contracts, yet no existing method determines which comparisons survive the reversal. We address this gap with contract-explicit evaluation: a preregistered five-step protocol (Declare, Measure, Scope, Certify, Hedge), operationalizing the classical concordance decomposition of Kendall's rank correlation, that scopes certifiable regions and delivers distribution-free census certificates across two ecosystems. In the DocRE audit (44 training runs of one in-house architecture family), the scoring dimension scopes to a census certificate (three flagged instances, Clopper--Pearson upper bound 0.146); the confirmatory record includes registered negatives, and the audit prices its own simplification finding---the calibration dial's entire margin is one withdrawn commit. In an LLM-judge census (17 judges, 49,938 battles), 12.25% of leaderboard comparisons require hedging at the pre-declared split criterion (bound 0.124; panel-robust 0.143), with an exploratory two-tier reading certifying 69% at a bound \le 0.072 and a validity decomposition against released human labels (65% of contested battles are judge error, not ambiguity). The cross-model certificate is withdrawn on real confidence scores; the failure spectrum maps the boundary. The protocol, map, ledger, and per-instance artifacts are released.

title: The Between-Round Decision in Autonomous Research: An LLM Controller That Reads the Whole Trajectory
summary: Executing an idea often changes how promising it looks, so the next step in autonomous research should rest on results, not on proposals. After each round of experiments, the system must decide whether to refine the best solution or start a new direction, which solution to build from, and what goal to set. We call this the between-round decision. Existing systems wrap it in machinery such as rules, scores, search trees, and schedules; where an LLM makes it, what the LLM needs to read is left open. We ask whether an LLM can make this decision from accumulated evidence, without a search structure around it, and how much of that evidence it needs to read. We present BRED (Between-Round Evidence-based Decision), an LLM-based controller that maintains the best verified solution so far (the Champion) and a log of past rounds, and makes one decision per round. On three widely used research-agent benchmark tasks, BRED improves on the task baselines by 4.80% in MAE on ETTh1 (to 0.4172) and by 3.44 and 3.43 points of accuracy on SST-2 (to 95.07%) and CIFAR-100 (to 84.63%), ahead of the published results. When the controller does not read the accumulated evidence, the same loop gains less: with no history it reaches 0.4299 on ETTh1 and 83.71% on CIFAR-100, whereas the full controller's MAE is 2.95% lower and its accuracy 0.92 points higher. On a new task, speech-based depression detection under a leakage-free protocol, it reaches a macro-F1 of 0.6164 on seeds held out from selection, 5.5 points above its baseline and 4.0 above the strongest published system. Code is available at https://github.com/learninginvision/BRED.

title: AlignedHPO: Efficient Surrogate-Guided Loss Hyperparameter Optimization
summary: Modern deep learning losses involve multiple hyperparameters, such as weights, scales, and margins, typically tuned manually or through expensive black-box optimization despite their differentiability. We propose AlignedHPO, an efficient framework for tuning differentiable loss hyperparameters using gradient alignment and surrogate validation objectives. Our method employs Jacobian-vector products to reduce hypergradient computation time and memory, while differentiable metric surrogates guide optimization toward task-specific evaluation criteria. We address gradient magnitude ambiguity and stochastic instability through normalized alignment and gradient smoothing. Experiments with generalized Focal Loss and ArcFace demonstrate effective adaptation across long-tailed classification and open-set face recognition. AlignedHPO achieves competitive or improved performance compared to implicit differentiation, with nearly 12x faster hypergradient computation. These results highlight the potential of efficient surrogate-guided loss hyperparameter optimization.

title: SpatialCast: Reading the 3D World via Cast Shadows
summary: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) advance toward understanding and interacting with the physical world, spatial reasoning becomes essential for understanding scene structure and anticipating the effects of physical changes. Existing spatial benchmarks have made substantial progress in evaluating spatial relations, memory, and viewpoint reasoning, but less systematically assess how models connect physical scene conditions with visual observations. We introduce SpatialCast, a benchmark that uses cast shadows to evaluate this ability. Cast shadows provide observable evidence of a 3D scene. Their image appearance depends on object geometry and pose, illumination, and viewpoint. We examine this relationship through three complementary tasks that assess scene-projection consistency, predict intervention-induced changes, and infer the physical changes behind visual transitions. The benchmark contains 21,000 synthetic questions with separate scene and geometry test partitions, complemented by 200 SpatialCast-Real questions from 20 photographed scenes. Evaluations show that closed-source MLLMs outperform general-purpose open-weight MLLMs and MLLMs designed for spatial reasoning, which remain near chance on the synthetic benchmark, while even strong closed-source models struggle with shadow-length and light-height judgments. We also use SpatialCast training data for GRPO post-training, improving open-weight MLLM performance on the benchmark. Further evaluations show improvements on several external spatial benchmarks, suggesting transfer of the learned capabilities. These experiments support SpatialCast as a controlled resource for diagnosing spatial reasoning capabilities and studying their learning and generalization.

title: VideoGym: An Adaptive RL Environment for Long-Video Agents
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) trains video agents to locate sparse evidence for long-video question answering through structured memory retrieval and temporal re-observation. This training, however, faces a long-tail modality distribution in the data. In our source pool, text-heavy questions account for 58% of samples, compared with 15% graph-heavy, 17% visual-heavy, and 10% time-range questions. Fixed-distribution RL therefore allocates fewer rollouts to underperforming question types. Reweighting these types could increase their sampling frequency but repeatedly reuses the same finite banks of original questions. To solve this problem, we introduce VideoGym, a curriculum-based RL environment that jointly constructs video-grounded training tasks and allocates rollouts among them. Within the environment, a memory-augmented VideoAgent is trained to coordinate retrieval from text, graph, and visual memories with temporal re-observation. Across episodes, VideoGym adapts VideoAgent's training distribution online: it casts per-period sample selection as an adversarial bandit over (modality, mode) arms and applies the EXP3 update to shift sampling toward arms with low answer accuracy. To supply the augmented-mode arms, a TaskGenerator-Verifier pipeline produces harder variants of existing questions that remain answerable within the same video. Across five long-video benchmarks, VideoGym lifts RL accuracy from 60.4% to 64.8% on average and by up to 10.5 pp on underrepresented graph-heavy questions with 3.3x sample efficiency. Together, these results show that task expansion and adaptive allocation can improve video agent learning from limited, imbalanced training data.

title: Scale-Aware Reference Attention for Mannequin-to-Model Gown Generation
summary: Formal gowns are sold online with photos of models wearing them, and buyers zoom in to inspect sequins, lace and beading. Image editors can turn a photo of a gown on a mannequin into a convincing photo of a person wearing it, but they receive every reference photo without any notion of its magnification, and the fine detail of the gown is lost when the output is viewed up close. We propose scale-aware reference attention (SARA), which tells an open diffusion transformer the zoom level of the output and of every reference photo, biases the attention of the output toward references of a similar zoom level, uses macro photos of the fabric as references, and is trained on a mix of whole-garment and zoomed targets. To train and evaluate it, we introduce Kiss3000, a dataset of 915 high-resolution mannequin photos and 2274 on-model photos of formal gowns with cross-domain pairs and splits by style, and zoom-crop evaluation, which compares garment crops at full, half and local scale without pixel alignment and judges local fidelity with two vision-language models gated on control crops. With this protocol, Nano Banana Pro at 4K, the highest-resolution commercial editor we test, loses or redraws local detail on 14 of 20 test gowns. At 1536x2048 pixels, both judges prefer SARA over a LoRA fine-tuning baseline on 18 test items and the baseline on 6 (p=0.023), and over the base model on 26 against 4 (p=5.9e-5), while SARA keeps the gown design as often as the baseline.

title: OmniTongue: A Comprehensive MLLM Benchmark for Automated Tongue Diagnosis in Traditional Chinese Medicine
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have excelled in Western medical imaging, yet their potential in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) tongue diagnosis remains systematically unevaluated. Tongue diagnosis requires sophisticated global and local perception, serving as a rigorous touchstone for assessing the visual understanding depth of MLLMs. However, existing datasets are limited by single dimensions, coarse granularity, and ambiguous labels, hindering the evaluation of authentic clinical capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce OmniTongue, the first comprehensive, fine-grained Visual Question Answering benchmark for TCM tongue diagnosis. This benchmark integrates 1,351 expert-validated images and 21,616 instruction pairs. Its core design features 16 clinical dimensions for multidimensional evaluation, region-specific annotations for pathological localization, and 66 fine-grained labels for precise diagnostic representation. Extensive evaluations of existing MLLMs reveal significant performance gaps, demonstrating that medical-specific models lack domain advantages, while universally poor Macro-F1 scores expose a reliance on statistical shortcuts rather than genuine understanding of tongue pathology. These findings not only highlight the current limitations of MLLMs in interpreting regional medical features but also underscore OmniTongue's significance for developing robust automated tongue diagnosis models. The code and dataset will be made publicly available in a future release.

title: Non-Intrusive Rubin Substructuring for Geometrically Nonlinear Structures via Nonlinear Manifolds
summary: Component mode synthesis enables modular reduction of large structural models, but its extension to geometrically nonlinear systems remains challenging. This work generalizes the Rubin method by introducing a cubic displacement manifold that statically condenses high-frequency free-interface modes onto the retained low-frequency modes and residual attachment modes. The reduced equations of motion, with cubic polynomial restoring forces, are derived by Galerkin projection onto the manifold tangent subspace. The consistency of the reduced forces is guaranteed by the cubic expansion of the component-level reduced manifold. We further present a non-intrusive procedure that combines elastic-force identification with finite-difference estimates of tangent-stiffness derivatives, which allows the reduced model to be constructed from the linear Rubin model and tangent-stiffness evaluations. In the proposed numerical tests, the reduced assembled models accurately reproduce the nonlinear responses of the full finite-element models, including internal resonance and modal coupling. Scalability and significant computational gains are demonstrated with an industrial scale model of a wing-box tip tank assembly, for which an online speed-up of about 24,666 was obtained.

title: Must You See Fakes to Catch Fakes? Language Says What to Look For, Real Images What to Ignore
summary: Must a detector see generated images in order to catch them? Detection of AI-generated images has long faced two problems. The cues a detector learns from the few generators in its training set carry traces specific to those generators and transfer poorly to new ones, which limits generalization. The real and generated training images also differ in format and content, so the detector takes these differences as evidence of authenticity, and its decisions change with factors that have nothing to do with authenticity, which harms robustness as well as generalization. Both problems stem from training on generated images. A detector never trained on them can largely avoid both at the source. Vision foundation models have already learned the concept of "AI-generated" during pretraining, and text can point to it directly. Building on this, we propose SaySee, a training-free detector: Say builds a generation direction from sets of paired descriptions that differ only in authenticity and scores an image by the projection of its embedding onto it, and See uses real images to correct the score offsets caused by format, image type and content. On 24 evaluation sets that span standard benchmarks, in-the-wild data and the latest generators, SaySee reaches a mean AUC of 98.2% with MoE-ViE, 4.2 points above the best existing detector. When format is decoupled from authenticity, it remains the best of all methods. Code will be released.

title: Inflation with an Exponential Power-Law Potential:Analytical Slow-Roll Relations, Branch Dynamics, and Conditional Reheating Matching
summary: We study canonical single-field inflation driven by the potential $V(φ)=M^4\exp(φ/M_{\rm Pl})(1+kφ/M_{\rm Pl})^{-1/k}$ with $k<0$. We retain the canonical Einstein--scalar action and derive analytical relations within the slow-roll approximation. Expressing the local spectra through the logarithmic slope $A=kx/(1+kx)$, with $x=φ/M_{\rm Pl}$, yields an endpoint-independent consistency relation among the scalar tilt, tensor ratio, and running at their stated approximation orders. On the negative-field branch, an exact phase-space argument shows that an initially downhill, inflationary hilltop trajectory cannot end inflation within the bare single-field model. We specify the endpoint as a phenomenological input and use a Lambert-$W$ solution of the slow-roll e-fold integral. Tables and figures illustrate the fixed choice $x_e=-2$ and must be interpreted conditionally on a completion that implements this endpoint and preserves the adiabatic spectrum. The reheating-matching relation uses explicit scale and thermal conventions and imposes both endpoint energy bounds and nonnegative reheating duration. The observational comparison uses published marginalized intervals rather than reconstructed joint posteriors. These results establish local analytical structure and conditional numerical benchmarks. A complete exit mechanism, a unique reheating equation of state, and precision spectral predictions remain unestablished.

title: Systematic Mapping Protocol. Generative AI-Augmented Requirements Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study of Practices, Specifications, and Reuse in Software Development
summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), particularly large language models (LLMs), is rapidly being adopted in requirements engineering (RE). Existing secondary studies have characterized which RE activities are supported and which prompting strategies are used, but little is known about the specifications that GenAI-augmented RE produces and how they are used in subsequent activities such as specification-driven development (SDD), design and code generation, test derivation, verification, and reuse. This document presents the protocol of a systematic mapping study (SMS) that will identify and classify research on GenAI-augmented RE, with particular attention to the work products it generates and their downstream use. The protocol defines the research questions and their classification schemes, the search strategy, the study selection procedure, the data extraction form, the analysis approach, the tool support, and the threats to validity. It is published in advance to establish a prior commitment and to support the transparency and repeatability of the study.

title: Sub-Meter Canopy Height Synthesis from Sentinel-2 via Anchored Residual Flow
summary: Canopy height models (CHMs) - per-pixel maps of vegetation top height - are essential for forest carbon accounting, wildfire fuel mapping, and tree-level ecology, yet sub-meter CHMs require airborne LiDAR refreshed on multi-year national cycles. We produce 0.5 m CHMs from free 10 m Sentinel-2 imagery, a 20$\times$ cross-modal super-resolution task where optical reflectance must predict geometric height it does not directly observe. Motivated by the perception-distortion trade-off, we derive two operating points with shared conditioning. A deterministic regressor (Anchor) targets low distortion; a conditional flow matching model, trained on the Anchor's residual in a learned CHM latent space (AR-flow), targets perceptual fidelity. Trained on 197k LiDAR-paired tiles spanning 69 ecoregions across the contiguous United States and evaluated on 2,530 held-out tiles against eight baselines, the Anchor achieves 2.83 m MAE using only free satellite input. The AR-flow reduces sliced Wasserstein distance from the Anchor's 1.13 to 0.208, at a higher MAE of 3.68 m. Crown-scale statistics improve, but strict individual-tree detection remains weak: generated sub-pixel detail represents plausible structure rather than measured individual trees. Quarterly continental refresh becomes tractable, letting satellite monitoring inform timing and extent for more expensive data acquisitions.

title: Prior-guided adaptive local refinement of foundation interatomic potentials
summary: Foundation interatomic potentials enable simulations across diverse materials, but task-specific inaccuracies can require additional first-principles data. Obtaining these data is challenging when the relevant local environments arise in large simulation cells. Here we introduce the Prior-guided Adaptive Refinement Scheme (PARS), which identifies weakly supported environments during molecular dynamics by comparing their frozen representations with prototypes of pretraining environments, without requiring initial task labels or model ensembles. Selected environments are reconstructed as compact periodic cells for first-principles labelling and iterative refinement. Applications to phase stability, surface migration and vacancy clustering show improvements in target properties, including an 81% reduction in the mean absolute error of Ti vacancy-cluster energies per vacancy relative to the pretrained model. For Si/Ge, a foundation potential refined using 800 labelled cells containing 10-128 atoms is subsequently distilled into a compact potential without additional first-principles training labels. In simulations containing approximately 362,880 atoms, the distilled model predicts an interfacial thermal resistance consistent with that of a potential trained directly on density-functional theory data. These results demonstrate a route for adapting foundation potentials to target applications through local reference calculations.

title: Stochastic Representation-Inspired Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Incompressible Fluid Flows
summary: The effectiveness of neural networks in solving partial differential equations depends not only on their approximation capability but also on the suitability of their representations for the underlying solutions. Motivated by stochastic integral representations of incompressible fluid flows and the associated Biot--Savart kernel, we propose a Biot--Savart-informed (i.e. physics-informed) neural network (BS-PINN) for the incompressible Navier--Stokes equations. By extracting a rational profile from a regularized Biot--Savart kernel, we construct a smooth activation function with fixed and learnable kernel scales. Both variants retain the conventional velocity--pressure formulation and physics-informed training framework, allowing the influence of the activation function to be examined independently. We evaluate the method on five benchmarks, including Kovasznay flow, cylinder wake, three-dimensional Beltrami flow, Taylor--Green vortex, and double shear layer. Across 21 benchmark--architecture comparisons, both variants consistently reduce the combined velocity error relative to the conventional $\tanh$-based PINN, achieving mean relative error reductions of 31.7\% and 33.2\%, respectively. Improvements are also observed in reported pressure and vorticity errors. Notably, the double-shear-layer experiments demonstrate improved resolution of localized shear structures and, for BS-PINN-F, qualitatively clearer vortex-roll-up patterns in the long-time simulation. These findings highlight the potential of incorporating analytical flow structures into neural-network representations for incompressible flow simulations.

title: What Do LLMs Use to Judge Synthesis Recipes? An Experimental Analysis on 240 Solid-State Syntheses
summary: Inorganic materials discovery is increasingly limited by synthesis rather than by material design. Large language models (LLMs) are being adopted to propose synthesis conditions with little experimental evidence of their capabilities and biases. Here, we carry out an experimental synthesis benchmark of 240 experiments across eight known and unknown inorganic oxides and subsequently evaluate an LLM as a zero-shot ranker over fixed banks of solid-state synthesis recipes. For each pair of recipes for the same oxide target, `GPT-5.6-Sol` selects the recipe expected to yield higher target-phase purity. We aggregate these pairwise preferences using a regularized Bradley-Terry model to obtain a ranked list of synthesis recipes for a given target material. By comparison with the actual purity, obtained through X-ray diffraction, we measure `GPT-5.6-Sol`'s performance as a zero-shot ranker (0.72 pairwise accuracy). By selective removal of the information exposed to the model during this ranking, we conclude that ranking is driven predominantly by thermal features, with reaction chemistry modulating the effect. Ranking accuracy tracks the purity-temperature correlation by target (Spearman ρ= 0.91\), \(p = 0.002\), and on the six thermally-driven targets withholding all chemical identity hardly impacts performance (0.68) compared to withholding temperature (0.56). Ranking performance was higher on known than unknown targets, but the group-level difference was not statistically conclusive. The methodological choices highlight the need for more experimentally validated synthesis benchmarks and position LLMs as a thermally informed prior.

title: Right Diagnosis, Unsafe Route: Auditing Clinical AI Decision Trajectories and Corrective Oversight for Validity and Potential Harm
summary: A clinical AI system can reach a correct final diagnosis through intermediate decisions that could have harmed the patient, and can repair an error while introducing new risks. Most evaluations score final diagnoses; even stepwise benchmarks, which release a case's evidence over time, score whether systems reach the right diagnosis or gather the right information, not whether the decisions a patient passes through are safe. We make patient safety the target of stepwise evaluation. A trajectory audit replays real admissions checkpoint by checkpoint, lets each system decide with only the evidence released so far, and rates every test, treatment and disposition for its potential harm to the patient and, separately, for clinical validity, against the documented final diagnosis and physician-written disease rubrics yet on the evidence available when the decision was made. An LLM judge scores every decision, and a physician reference standard (triple annotation and senior adjudication of a stratified sample) calibrates the rates. An oversight audit branches each trajectory at its first actionable error and measures, on the same branches, whether corrective feedback repairs the error and whether it introduces new harm. Across 300 cases from a hospital cardiology cohort, MIMIC-IV and the public ASCENT benchmark, with up to seven AI systems per source, 55.2% of hospital trajectories reaching an acceptable final diagnosis passed through a decision with moderate or severe potential harm and 24.8% through a clinically unacceptable one; the harm rates were 76.2% on MIMIC-IV and 39.6% on ASCENT. Structured corrections resolved 73.6% of first errors versus 24.8% after bare rejection, yet new potentially unsafe decisions followed 30.2% of corrections versus 19.7% of rejections. A correct final diagnosis does not certify a safe trajectory, and a successful correction does not certify a safe recovery.

title: EvoSkill-S1: Evolving Reusable Skills with Genetic-Inspired Operators
summary: Reusable skills allow language-model agents to accumulate and reuse problem-solving experience. However, most existing methods improve a skill bank only indirectly through rollout-driven accumulation and heuristic reflection, often resulting in shallow and weakly controlled updates. We present EvoSkill-S1, an RL-driven framework that instead treats reusable skills themselves as the direct objects of evolution. Given hard-negative failures, EvoSkill-S1 selects parent skills and transforms them into candidate child skills through five genetic-inspired operators: revision, cross-revision, mutation, dual-reflection, and crossover. Downstream task rewards train the skill evolver to generate more effective child skills, while evaluator-guided write-back selectively retains beneficial updates. Complementary Skill Bank Fusion consolidates operator-specific banks to exploit their distinct recovery patterns, while a Procedural Skill Interface supports transfer to unseen problems. Across all reported math and code benchmarks, EvoSkill-S1 improves the corresponding initialized skill banks under both Qwen and GPT-family solvers, with relative gains of up to 12.39%. Compared with the strongest external baseline without direct skill evolution, the largest relative improvement reaches 20.39%.

title: VidRouteBench: A Benchmark for Budgeted Video-Generation Routing
summary:
Text-to-video generators differ by two orders of magnitude in price, and a cheap configuration of a strong model is often good enough for a prompt. Routing prompts across such arms (model x sampling configuration) should buy quality at fixed budget, but no dataset supports studying it: public video-preference sets contain only closed models, one configuration each.
  We release VidRouteBench: 16 arms from 7 open families spanning 121x in measured cost ($0.0025-$0.298 per clip), 27,110 clips (1,421 A800-hours) over 1,625 grouped prompts, a quality score frozen after calibration against human preferences (68.7% CV accuracy vs 66.2% for the best single scorer), per-clip scores on 9 identifiable quality dimensions, repeated seeds, an encrypted test split, and a sealed newest family for cold start. The evaluator compares a router against the best prompt-agnostic mixture of arms, not the best single arm. Per-prompt specialisation here is real and predictable (oracle gap 0.642, 47% reproducible across seeds, prompt-arm interaction F=4.47 at p=1.6e-63), unlike LLM-routing arms, where the same pipeline finds none.
  We then propose OPMU (one probe, many utilities): label a new arm on K probe prompts, predict its 9 dimensions once, and serve any scenario utility by scalarising afterwards. Over 215 utility directions OPMU Pareto-dominates the prompt-agnostic baseline for 94% of directions versus 90% for per-scenario routers, with no per-scenario retraining. Three baselines fail instructively: bag-of-words features lose almost all routing gain in the low-data regime (0.009 vs 0.168); crediting a new arm with its probe average is harmful (-3.32 recovery) although it is the strong baseline on RewardBench-style arms (0.786); Chebyshev scalarisation does not help, our cost-utility front being convex.

title: A comprehensive Sun-as-a-star catalog of interplanetary type-III bursts: Statistics and a framework for stellar exospace weather applications
summary: Decameter-hectometric (DH) type-III bursts, produced by energetic electron beams escaping into interplanetary (IP) space, are often associated with strong soft X-ray (SXR) flares, coronal mass ejections (CMEs), and solar energetic particle events (SEPEs). With future DH missions being planned, these intense bursts could provide reliable exospace weather event diagnostics, given the lack of direct stellar IP particle and CME probes. We present a catalog of DH type-III bursts associated with 538 out of 734 $\geq$C5-class flares observed by Wind and STEREO spacecraft during 2006-2025. Independent of the SXR flare strength, the occurrence and Sun-as-a-star emission properties of DH type-III bursts distinguish confined flares, CMEs with and without strong IP shocks, and SEPEs.
